summary: Proposes an indexed text encoding for the SIP Common Log Format that keeps the advantages of a text format while making it faster to process. It is the concrete format for the framework in RFC 6872.

plainLanguage.summary: This document says how to write SIP server logs so that a program can jump straight to the field it wants. The log stays plain text, so the usual command line tools still work on it.

subtitle: A fast-to-search, still human-readable file format for logging SIP messages.

tldr.problem: Web servers have a well-known text log format, but the text format is slow to process when a log is large, and SIP messages carry more structure than HTTP requests.
tldr.mechanism: The document defines a SIP log record with a 60-byte header of index pointers that say where each field sits, followed by tab-separated mandatory fields and optional extensions.
tldr.outcome: It is a Proposed Standard from February 2013, updated by RFC 7355, and it is the concrete file format for the SIP logging framework in RFC 6872.

facts.label: Transport flag values
facts.value: U for UDP, T for TCP, S for SCTP

today: RFC 6873 is a Proposed Standard published in February 2013. It is updated by RFC 7355 and has not been obsoleted, so it remains the file format for SIP Common Log Format records.

sections.title: Why a SIP Log Format
sections.content:
The Apache Common Log Format (CLF) and its wide adoption prompted the development of an analogous event logging mechanism for the Session Initiation Protocol (RFC 3261). Implementing a logging scheme for SIP is a considerable challenge. Part of that is the behaviour of a SIP entity being more complex than that of an HTTP entity. There are also shortcomings in the purely text-based HTTP CLF that need to be addressed so that SIP log files can be inspected in real time, as described in RFC 6872. Experience with Apache CLF has shown that dealing with large quantities of log data can be very processor intensive, because it necessarily requires reading and parsing every byte of the files of interest.

The framework for the SIP CLF was already defined in RFC 6872. This document describes an indexed text file format for logging SIP messages received and sent by SIP clients, servers and proxies, and it adheres to the information model in Section 8 of RFC 6872. The format is no more difficult for a logging entity to generate than a standard non-indexed text log format, while being far faster to process. It is optimised for rapidly scanning through log records and quickly locating commonly accessed data fields. It also keeps the key advantage of being human readable and processable with Unix text tools such as sed, awk, perl, cut and grep.
sections.plainLanguage: Ordinary web logs are plain text, but reading every byte of them is slow when they get big. This format adds a small table of contents at the front of each record so a program can go straight to the part it needs.

sections.title: The Three Parts of a Record
sections.content:
The format of a SIP CLF record can be logically subdivided into three components, even though there is no actual subdivision in practice.

The Index Pointers are the first 60 bytes of the format. They are metadata, mostly a list of pointers that say where the variable-length mandatory and optional fields start. They exist to improve processing of the records and to let a reader skip directly to the field it wants without going through the whole record. A line feed character delimits this part from the next.

The Mandatory Fields are a tab-separated listing of the mandatory fields described in Section 8.1 of RFC 6872, in the order listed by the index pointers. The Optional Fields are the last component and are an optional extension to the format. They give the developer of a SIP CLF the freedom to log any desired field that is not in the mandatory list, which includes SIP bodies and vendor-specific extensions.

In a log file the record appears as two lines, with the index pointer metadata on one line and the data, mandatory and optional, on the next. The record ends with a line feed. Figures 1 and 2 of the document, plus that terminating line feed, are different representations of the same thing.
sections.plainLanguage: Each record has three parts: a table of contents, the fields that every record must have, and any extra fields the operator wants to add.

sections.title: The Index Pointers
sections.content:
The Version field is one byte, a UTF-8 encoded version for the SIP CLF record. Valid values run from 'A' (0x41) to 'Z' (0x5A), and this document uses 0x41. The value MUST be incremented for any new SIP CLF specification that changes any part of the record format, and the values are IANA-assigned through the Standards Action method described in RFC 5226. Because the version is specified per record, a log file could in principle hold records with different versions, which under normal operating conditions is unlikely and SHOULD be avoided.

The Record Length field is six bytes, a hexadecimal encoded total length of the log record from the Version octet to the terminating line feed. Bytes 8 through 55 hold hexadecimal encoded pointers to the start of each variable-length mandatory field, and bytes 56 through 59 hold the pointer to the start of the optional fields. There are no delimiters between the pointer values: they are packed together as a single 52-character hexadecimal string. The pointer values are absolute byte values within the record, and are therefore 82 or greater. They point to the start of the corresponding value in the mandatory fields portion.

The Optional Fields Start Pointer is the final pointer. It indicates where the optional group begins, and points at the tab character for the first entry there. If the optional group is not implemented, this field MUST point at the terminating line feed instead. Numbers in the format are always written in human-readable form, hexadecimal using the characters 0 through 9 and A through F, or decimal using 0 through 9, and always occupy the full number of bytes indicated, padded on the left with zeros.
sections.plainLanguage: The header says which version of the format the record uses, how long the record is, and where each field starts. A reader uses those numbers to jump straight to the field it wants.

sections.title: The Mandatory Fields
sections.content:
Two fixed-length fields follow the pointers and give the exact time of the log entry. The Timestamp is ten bytes, a decimal encoded date and time as the number of seconds since the Unix epoch. The Fractional Seconds field is three bytes, the fractional part of the timestamp to millisecond accuracy. Together they appear as a string of seconds and milliseconds separated by a full stop.

The Flags Field is five bytes. Byte one is the request and response flag, with R for a request and r for a response. Byte two is the retransmission flag, with O for an original transmission, D for a duplicate transmission and S meaning the server is stateless, so retransmissions are not detected. Byte three is the sent and received flag, with S for a sent message and R for a received one. Byte four is the transport flag, whose registered values are U for UDP, T for TCP and S for SCTP. Byte five is the encryption flag, with E for an encrypted message, such as one over TLS or DTLS, and U for an unencrypted one.

After the timestamp, fractional seconds and flags come the mandatory fields themselves, in the order given by the index pointers, and every one of them must be present. They are the CSeq header field including its number and method name; the response status code, which is a single dash for a request; the request URI from the start line, including any URI parameters; the destination IP address and port of the downstream server; the source IP address and port the message was received on; the URI and tag parameter from the To header; the URI and tag parameter from the From header; the Call-ID header value; the server transaction identifier; and the client transaction identifier. IPv4 addresses are written in dotted decimal and IPv6 addresses in hexadecimal notation enclosed in square brackets. Each field is subject to the maximum SIP CLF field size of 4096 bytes set out in Section 8 of RFC 6872.
sections.plainLanguage: Every record carries the time, five one-letter flags saying what kind of message it was, and a fixed list of fields such as the call identifier, the addresses and the URI. They always appear in the same order.

sections.title: Escaping and Encoding Rules
sections.content:
Mandatory fields are separated by a single tab character. Any tab characters inside the data being written are replaced by a space before the data is logged, because there is no standardized use of tabs in SIP headers to convey anything other than whitespace. Tabs may appear in message bodies, so this substitution can cause problems when a body is reconstructed from a log entry. Two consequences follow: it becomes impossible to reconstruct a signature over a logged field that matches the signature over the fields of the original message, and any future header field that uses a tab with a different meaning loses it when logged.

A field may not always have a value to log, even when it is required to appear. When a mandatory field is not present, it MUST be encoded as a single horizontal dash. When a field fails to parse, it MUST be encoded as a single question mark. If either of those characters would be the only character in a field, the implementation SHOULD insert the escaped forms %2D and %3F instead, so there is no ambiguity.

The terminating carriage return and line feed after a header field value MUST NOT be logged, and since a bare CRLF is not permitted inside a SIP header field value, no escaping is needed for it. A SIP parser could not parse a whole SIP CLF record successfully, though individual fields can be extracted and handed to a SIP parser. Any field modified by the escaping rules is likely no longer well-formed SIP and will fail that parser. The point of logging is not to recreate the exact message: the rules may lose information, and a reader should never unescape anything in the record, since it is meant to be processed by text tools such as grep and awk.
sections.plainLanguage: Fields are separated by tabs, and a tab inside the data is turned into a space. A missing field is written as a dash and an unreadable one as a question mark, so nothing is lost silently.

sections.title: Optional Fields
sections.content:
After the mandatory fields there may be zero or more optional field groups. Each is written as Tag@Vendor-ID,Length,BEB,Value. The identifier is a two-byte tag and an eight-byte vendor ID, both decimal encoded and separated by an at sign. It is modelled loosely on the private use option of the syslog protocol (RFC 5424), and it uses the Private Enterprise Number, which provides an identifier through a globally unique name space. This gives the format the extensibility to log any SIP header, body or vendor-specified element.

A vendor ID of zero is used for the standard optional elements. Tag 00 logs a SIP header field or the Reason-Phrase: the value holds the whole header field, its name, the colon and the field value, and a Reason-Phrase is written as the name, a colon and a space and then the phrase. Tag 01 logs the message body, and there can be only one such entry; the value holds the Content-Type followed by a space and then the body, and the body must be truncated if it would exceed the 4096 byte field limit. Tag 02 logs the entire SIP message, again with only one entry allowed. A vendor ID set to the vendor's own private enterprise number is used for any vendor-specified element, with the tag chosen by the implementer.

The Base64 Encoded Byte is a boolean saying whether the value is Base64 encoded. A value MUST be Base64 encoded if it has any unprintable characters, meaning an octet with a value from 0 to 31, an octet with a value of 127, or any series of octets of 128 or above that do not form valid UTF-8. If the value is Base64 encoded the flag is 0x01, otherwise 0x00. Any carriage return and line feed in a logged body MUST be escaped as the URI encoded equivalent %0D%0A, and a body that is Base64 encoded must be encoded before any character escaping.
sections.plainLanguage: Anything else worth logging can be added after the standard fields. Each extra item says what it is, who defined it, how long it is, and whether its bytes were turned into safe text.

sections.title: Security and Operational Guidance
sections.content:
The document introduces no new security considerations beyond those in RFC 6872. It does repeat one of them: because a SIP CLF file contains sensitive information, values might need to be obfuscated for privacy reasons when the file is exchanged between domains. If a Base64 encoded string contains a non-obfuscated value, that value would also need to be obfuscated before the Base64 encoding.

On operations, SIP CLF log files will take up a substantive amount of disk space depending on the traffic volume at a processing entity and the amount of information being logged, so any enterprise using SIP CLF should establish procedures for file rollovers suited to its needs. Listing such guidelines in the document is out of scope.

The format is also designed so that text tools do not need to understand the indexing. Index lines always start with an alphabetical character and field lines with a numerical one, so index lines can be discarded by checking the first character. Within a field line, script tools can split on the tabs: the first 12 fields are positional, and the meaning of later fields can be found from the first four characters of the field or with a regular expression.
sections.plainLanguage: Log files can hold personal information, so they should be scrubbed before being passed to another organisation, and they get big enough that rotating them needs planning.

fields.name: Version
fields.desc: Format version, from 'A' to 'Z'. This document uses 0x41.

fields.name: Record Length
fields.desc: First part of the hexadecimal total length of the record.

fields.name: Record Length (cont)
fields.desc: Second part of the hexadecimal total length.

fields.name: Delimiter
fields.desc: 0x2C, the comma that ends the length field.

fields.name: Response Status-Code Pointer
fields.desc: Where the response status code starts.

fields.name: Server-Txn Pointer
fields.desc: Where the server transaction identifier starts.

fields.name: Client-Txn Pointer
fields.desc: Where the client transaction identifier starts.

fields.name: Optional Fields Start Pointer
fields.desc: Where the optional fields begin, or the final line feed if there are none.

items.label: HEADER FIELD
items.desc: A SIP header field, or the Reason-Phrase of a response.

items.label: MESSAGE BODY
items.desc: The body of the message, with its Content-Type. Only one per record.

items.label: ENTIRE MESSAGE
items.desc: The whole SIP message. Only one per record.
